title: Adaptive devices: Planned changes preserve regulatory control
desc: Allows bounded AI-device modification through prospective testing and risk controls, retaining lifecycle evidence and fresh review outside authorized scope.

kps.k: FDA offers bounded, prospective authorization of AI-device updates rather than unrestricted permission to change deployed systems.
kps.d: The final guidance presents Predetermined Change Control Plans (PCCPs) as a way to reduce repeated premarket submissions while maintaining safety and effectiveness. Under section 515C of the FD&C Act, manufacturers can implement specified changes without fresh authorization only when FDA has authorized the plan with the device and implementation follows that plan. Existing approval, clearance and scientific-evidence standards remain intact. The guidance supplies recommendations, not new binding requirements except where it cites statute or regulation.

qs.q: 32 The recommendations in this guidance do not change applicable statutory and regulatory standards, such as device clearance or approval standards, nor the applicable requirements, including marketing submission content requirements and the requirements for valid scientific evidence.
qs.a: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited.

kps.k: Regulatory flexibility depends on specifying changes, testing and risk controls before deployment.
kps.d: FDA recommends linking a limited set of specific, testable modifications to a Modification Protocol and Impact Assessment. Protocols should cover data management, retraining, performance evaluation and deployment, using predefined acceptance criteria and representative test data independent of training and tuning data. Manufacturers should record unresolvable evaluation failures and block the affected update. Impact assessments should examine individual changes, unintended bias, interactions and cumulative effects across the device, rather than rely solely on an improved performance metric.

qs.q: As part of a marketing submission, the manufacturer should provide a PCCP, consisting of a Description of Modifications (Section VI.), a Modification Protocol (Section VII.), and an Impact Assessment (Section VIII.).
qs.a: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Test data should be independent of data used for training and tuning and should generally be from multiple sites different from those that were used to generate training and tuning data.
qs.a: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance) · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: The framework accommodates adaptation, but eligibility remains device-specific and constrained by intended use.
kps.d: Potentially eligible modifications include performance improvements, input compatibility and some subpopulation adaptations. Changes must preserve intended use and, where applicable, substantial equivalence; FDA generally recommends preserving indications for use but allows some exceptions. Automatic updates and local adaptation are not categorically excluded, although FDA calls for explicit boundaries, deployment conditions and update frequencies. Its practical review experience predominantly concerns machine learning, which qualifies the guidance’s broader application to AI-enabled devices.

qs.q: Modifications included in a PCCP must maintain the device within the device’s intended use, 91 and as applicable, must allow the device to remain substantially equivalent to the predicate device.
qs.a: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: 94 However, there may be certain modifications to the indications for use (e.g., certain changes in the indications for use to specify use of the device with an additional device or component) that may be appropriate for inclusion in a PCCP.
qs.a: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance) · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Conformity with the authorized scope and methods—not performance alone—determines whether fresh review is needed.
kps.d: FDA treats a modification as conforming only when the plan specifies it and the manufacturer follows the authorized protocol. Significant out-of-plan changes and departures from protocol methods likely require a new submission; revising the PCCP itself generally also requires review. FDA warns that deviations can cause adulteration and misbranding and invite enforcement. Choosing not to implement an authorized change, pursuing a separate submission, or making a change that needs no submission does not itself constitute a deviation.

qs.q: Manufacturers should first consider whether the particular modification is or is not consistent with the authorized PCCP; FDA considers a modification to be consistent with the authorized PCCP when the modification has been specified in the Description of Modifications included in the PCCP and has been implemented in accordance with the Modification Protocol.
qs.a: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Significant modifications made to a device that are not specified in, or implemented in accordance with, the authorized PCCP likely require a new marketing submission.
qs.a: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance) · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Avoiding repeated submissions leaves manufacturers responsible for lifecycle evidence, traceability and user transparency.
kps.d: Manufacturers must document conforming changes through their quality systems. FDA recommends retaining evidence that would otherwise support a separate submission, maintaining version-controlled plans, and explaining updates, performance changes and effects on legacy users. Labeling should accurately describe available versions and site-specific modifications rather than imply that planned capabilities already exist. Post-market surveillance and appropriate user training complement predeployment testing. Early FDA engagement can help clarify a proposed plan, but consultation does not authorize it.

qs.q: Documentation of modifications verified and validated per the Modification Protocol must be compliant with the QSR, including that the manufacturer must document the change in accordance with the manufacturer’s quality system.
qs.a: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: 107 The available labeling should also reflect information about the current version(s) of the AI-DSF available to the user, including information regarding site-specific modifications.
qs.a: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance) · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: The source advances a regulatory design, not empirical proof that controlled updates reduce burdens or preserve safety.
kps.d: The supplied material presents FDA’s position rather than competing stakeholder arguments. Its central tension lies between enabling iterative improvement and retaining enforceable safety boundaries. FDA characterizes the approach as often least burdensome, but its device scenarios illustrate policy rather than report outcomes from authorized products. Examples involving new diagnostic functions or changed reference standards show why comparable measured performance does not establish plan conformity. The illustrative 20% processing-speed improvement should not be treated as an observed product result.

qs.q: This guidance describes an approach that would often be least burdensome for manufacturers to support the ability to modify an AI-DSF while maintaining the safety and effectiveness of the device across the intended use populations.
qs.a: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Due to the complexity of AI-DSFs, all examples are hypothetical and do not reflect any specific authorized device.
qs.a: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance) · Regulators & courts · 2024

vlens.an: The FDA guidance directly supports the proposition that adaptive AI-enabled devices can be updated without repeated premarket submissions only within prospectively authorized boundaries. Its regulatory rationale combines flexibility with continued control: proposed modifications must be specified in advance, validated under predefined protocols, assessed for individual and cumulative risk, documented through quality systems, and communicated transparently to users. Material variation lies in how much adaptation may qualify: automatic updates, local adaptations and some changes affecting indications may be eligible, but suitability depends on the device’s intended use and benefit-risk profile. Changes outside the authorized scope or methods generally return to fresh review. The source advances a regulatory framework rather than empirical evidence that it reduces burden or preserves safety in practice; its examples are hypothetical. Because the supplied evidence contains one FDA source, this position should not be generalized to all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: Significant modifications made to a device that are not specified in, or implemented in accordance with, the authorized PCCP likely require a new marketing submission.
qs.a: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance) · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The sole supplied source for the 2023–2024 period directly supports the proposition that adaptive AI-enabled medical devices can be updated without repeated submissions only within prospectively authorized and controlled boundaries. Its central reasoning is that a PCCP must specify intended modifications in advance and connect them to validation, acceptance criteria, risk assessment, quality-system documentation and user transparency; significant changes outside the authorized scope or protocol likely require a fresh marketing submission. Material internal variation concerns the breadth and status of that flexibility: the framework can accommodate automatic updates, local adaptation and some changes affecting indications, but eligibility is device-specific, constrained by intended use and benefit-risk considerations, and grounded largely in FDA’s experience with machine-learning devices. The guidance is principally a regulatory design and set of recommendations—not empirical evidence that PCCPs actually reduce burdens while preserving safety—and its scenarios are expressly hypothetical. Because the curated evidence contains one FDA source, it establishes that source’s position but does not indicate how prevalent the view was among regulators, manufacturers or other stakeholders in the period.
